analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal board to re-review foodmakers' old self-declared 'safe' rulings on food additives.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in late January 2026 with one Democratic cosponsor and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, a food company can decide on its own that an ingredient is 'generally recognized as safe' (GRAS) and never show the FDA its evidence. This bill targets the oldest of those self-declarations — ones made before 2000, including ones companies never told the FDA about. It creates a review board inside the Department of Health and Human Services, requires manufacturers to disclose every covered designation within 90 days, ranks them for review, and lets the Secretary revoke a designation if the company cannot prove within 180 days that the substance is actually safe, including ordering recalls.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of packaged and processed foods, since the bill would force the first federal review of additives that companies declared safe on their own, some decades ago and without ever showing the FDA their evidence. The public also gains transparency: the board must publish its findings and recommendations on the FDA website.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every food manufacturer, within 90 days of the bill becoming law, to identify to the board each covered GRAS designation attributable to it — including designations the company never filed with or notified to the FDA.

Directs the board to review the validity of each covered designation, tier them by priority, and report its findings to the Secretary, to Congress, and publicly on the FDA website — tier 1 within 2 years, tier 2 within 4, tier 3 within 10.

Lets the Secretary revoke a designation if the board finds the substance has not been shown to be safe, gives the manufacturer 180 days to produce sufficient scientific evidence of safety, and requires procedures for pulling the substance from distribution and recalling it if the revocation stands.

Gives the Secretary enforcement tools against companies that refuse to disclose their designations: civil penalties under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, or treating the undisclosed substance as an unapproved — and therefore unsafe — food additive.

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers, which must compile and disclose their ingredient designations, face civil penalties if they do not, and may have to reformulate products, stop distributing, and recall substances whose safety designations are revoked. Some of those compliance and reformulation costs would likely be passed on to consumers in prices.

drawbacks.text: The board's voting members are entirely government officials — the HHS and Agriculture Secretaries and staff from FDA, USDA, EPA, and their legal offices; the only outside expertise, an academic food toxicologist and a food industry representative, are non-voting members appointed by the Secretary. An independent-scientist review body this is not.

The scope is limited to designations made before 2000, so the many GRAS self-determinations companies have made since then — including the modern self-affirmation pathway the FDA tightened rules around — are left out of this review.

Revocation is discretionary ('may'), not mandatory: the Secretary can decline to act on a board recommendation that a substance has not been shown to be safe, and enforcement penalties attach only to failing to file a notice, not to the underlying safety of the ingredient.
The board and the entire Act terminate 10 years after enactment, so if the review is not completed — tier 3 reviews are due at the 10-year mark — part of it could expire unfinished.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but slow: Americans eat additives whose 'safe' status rests on company paperwork that was never independently reviewed, and this bill finally pulls that paperwork into public view and allows revocation. The costs are real but ordinary for a regulatory compliance exercise. The design is imperfect — an all-agency voting board, a pre-2000 cutoff, and discretionary revocation — so the bill is a partial fix to the GRAS loophole rather than a full one. On balance, the public-safety benefit plausibly outweighs the compliance cost, but the bill's narrow scope means the broader problem would remain.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it sits with no hearing, markup, or floor vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Lawler (R-NY) introduced the GRAS Oversight and Transparency Act on January 30, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The bill has one cosponsor, a Democrat, giving it small bipartisan sponsorship.
No further action has been taken since the referral — no committee vote, no hearing listed, no floor action.

The bill would direct HHS, through the FDA Commissioner, to create a board that reviews the validity of GRAS designations made by manufacturers before 2000, including designations never filed or notified to the FDA.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, food manufacturers: their decades-old self-declared safety rulings remain unreviewed by anyone, because the bill has not moved past referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food manufacturers, whose safety claims remain unreviewed

for.name: One Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's sole cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action since — no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship is bipartisan in form — a Republican sponsor with one Democratic cosponsor — but the bill is so early that no partisan voting pattern exists yet.

industries.note: The bill forces them to disclose every pre-2000 self-declared GRAS designation within 90 days, face civil penalties or 'unsafe food additive' treatment if they do not, and potentially reformulate, stop distribution, and recall substances whose designations are revoked. Their interest in keeping unreviewed safety designations intact runs against consumers' interest in having additives independently checked. The bill does give the industry one non-voting seat on the review board.

If designations come under review, manufacturers would need to generate and supply scientific safety evidence within 180-day windows, creating demand for independent safety testing. This gain only materializes if the bill advances and revocations actually occur.

analysis.trajectory: With only one cosponsor and no committee action since referral, the bill's likely path is to sit in Energy and Commerce and expire at the end of the 119th Congress, as most bills do. GRAS reform has drawn executive-branch attention, so a narrow path exists if leadership attaches the bill to a broader food-safety package, but nothing in the record suggests that is underway.
